title: The 20-minute emergency workout

Persistent unexplained tiredness, snoring with breathing pauses or repeated sleep disruption deserves medical advice, not a wearable-based diagnosis.
ACTION (10–20s): Preview a coach-approved workout option. Bring the recurring obstacle to your next check-in.

learning_design.science: Sleep is regulated by both sleep pressure and circadian timing. Regular sleep schedules and attention to light and caffeine can support the next sleep opportunity.

decision.question: How do you feel right now?

choices.label: Tired but functioning
choices.answer: Use the warm-up to assess technique and effort. Choose a coach-approved easier option if needed; avoid attempting a personal record.

choices.label: Sleepy enough to feel unsafe
choices.answer: Do not drive or perform hazardous training. Prioritise safety and arrange appropriate support.

choices.label: This keeps happening
choices.answer: Record the pattern and seek medical advice, especially with loud snoring, gasping or marked daytime sleepiness.

case.context: A late call leaves you short of sleep before a planned heavy session.
case.action: Assess alertness first. If safe but clearly under-recovered, choose an approved easier session and protect tonight’s bedtime.
case.reason: You reduce unnecessary risk without judging the whole programme by one night.

steps: Use how you feel and function, not only the watch score.
Avoid using late caffeine to force a normal evening.
Keep the next sleep window as regular as your schedule allows.
learning_design.takeaway: Protect safety today and the next sleep opportunity tonight.

title: Why body weight fluctuates
description: Look for a pattern before reacting to a single morning.
quick_answer: A single number is a measurement. A repeated pattern is more useful evidence.
body: Do not change targets because of one higher reading. Use the measurements already agreed with your coach and consider attendance, performance and how the routine is working too. If weighing creates distress, discuss another way to review progress. Rapid unexplained changes, swelling or other symptoms should be assessed by a clinician.

visual.title: A trend can hide inside daily noise

nodes.label: Water
nodes.text: Salt, carbohydrate storage and hormonal changes can alter water weight.

nodes.label: Contents
nodes.text: Food, fluids and bowel contents contribute to scale weight.

nodes.label: Tissue
nodes.text: Longer-term changes may include fat and lean tissue.

visual.caption: Illustrative measurements below are synthetic; they are not your data or a forecast.

learning_design.science: Body weight reflects multiple compartments. Short-term changes are not a direct measurement of body-fat change, so similar measurement conditions and repeated observations are more useful than one reading.
learning_design.limitation: A trend still cannot separate fat, muscle and fluid precisely. A flat week is not enough evidence to diagnose a fat-loss plateau.

choices.label: Up after a meal out
choices.answer: Return to normal meals and compare repeated readings under similar conditions. Do not immediately cut calories.

choices.label: A longer pattern has flattened
choices.answer: Review the trend, plan adherence, movement and measurement conditions with your coach before changing targets.

choices.label: Rapid unexplained change or symptoms
choices.answer: Seek medical advice for unexplained rapid changes, swelling or other concerning symptoms.

case.context: The scale rises after restaurant food even though the overall week has gone well.
case.action: Keep normal meals and review several comparable measurements rather than changing the plan that morning.
case.reason: You avoid mistaking a noisy observation for a change in body composition.

steps: If weighing, use comparable conditions and a schedule that is comfortable for you.
Consider training performance, waist measures and how clothes fit alongside weight.
Do not weigh more often if it worsens distress.
learning_design.takeaway: A single number is a measurement. A repeated pattern is more useful evidence.

title: Getting back on track after a difficult week
description: Do not wait for a clean Monday to repair a difficult week.
quick_answer: You do not need a new start date. You need a next action.
body: Use the existing planner rather than creating an ambitious catch-up schedule. Check whether the original week still fits your work and recovery. Pick one commitment you can keep and build from there. If an injury, illness or significant life event disrupted the routine, let your coach know before restarting the previous workload.

learning_design.headline: Restart at the next useful action.

visual.title: Make the restart specific

nodes.label: Choose
nodes.text: One action small enough to do today.

nodes.label: Place
nodes.text: Decide when and where it will happen.

nodes.label: Backup
nodes.text: Plan what you will do if work interrupts.

visual.caption: A planning framework, not a promise that habits form in a fixed number of days.

learning_design.science: Reviews suggest action and coping plans can help physical activity. Effects vary, and a field experiment found that simple scheduling alone did not reliably increase repeated gym attendance.
learning_design.limitation: Planning is a tool, not a guarantee. The action must be feasible, and recurring barriers need changes to the environment or programme.

choices.label: A meal is next
choices.answer: Eat the next assigned or suitable ordinary meal. Set up tomorrow’s lunch before the evening gets busy.

choices.label: A session is next
choices.answer: Attend the next realistic assigned session. Use an approved shorter option if the normal session does not fit.

choices.label: Everything feels too much
choices.answer: Pick one achievable action and tell your coach what changed. Simplify the week before adding more tasks.

case.context: A deadline derails training, meals and check-ins. You feel like waiting until Monday.
case.action: Today: eat the next normal meal. Tomorrow: attend one realistic session. If a call overruns, use the approved backup slot.
case.reason: The restart has a place in the diary and an alternative when work intervenes.

steps: Write: When ___ happens, I will ___ at ___.
Make the backup easier than the original action.
Review the barrier after the action, not before every restart.
learning_design.takeaway: You do not need a new start date. You need a next action.
